data.title: Is getting a wedding band from Quince a bad idea? It's a third of the price of a local jeweler.
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

'I am slightly anxious about purchasing something so big' from an online retailer known for cut-price duplicates of popular clothes and accessories

"Is there insurance for it, like there is for my actual ring?"

Dear Dollar Signs,

I recently got engaged and my ring was too big and the stone was loose. When we went to get it resized, the jeweler charged us $80, which I think is ridiculous because the stone was loose.

I was going to get my wedding bands from this same jeweler because I like that they are a local Chicago jeweler, but now we are thinking of getting our wedding bands from Quince. It's a third of the price, and the customer service at the local jewelry store wasn't even good.

However, I am slightly anxious about purchasing something so big through Quince. How does shipping work? Is there insurance for it, like there is for my actual ring?

Bride

If you're just starting out on your money or career journey and have questions about how to navigate your finances, we want to hear from you. Write to Dollar Signs, MarketWatch's new advice column, at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

Dear Bride,

I understand your hesitation: Buying a wedding ring online, without trying it on or seeing it in person, feels like a scam waiting to happen. Don't do anything that makes you uncomfortable, but I'd say Quince is a totally legitimate, safe place to purchase a wedding band.

For the uninitiated, Quince is a high-end, direct-to-consumer brand which makes duplicates of pricey, popular apparel and accessories. (To be totally transparent, I'll disclose that I bought a winter coat from Quince last year which was meant to be a duplicate of the Aritzia Super Puff. It is fantastic.)

Quince offers free standard shipping on all items, and you must sign to receive the package if it cost more than $100. While it doesn't offer insurance, all jewelry does come with a warranty that covers "imperfections that are the result of defects in the manufacturing process." (You can read more about the details of the warranty here.)

Like I said, don't do anything that makes you uneasy. But, I do believe that buying wedding bands and engagement rings online is an extension of Americans' growing preference to shop digitally instead of at brick-and-mortar stores: 28.4% of consumers prefer to do most or all of their shopping online, according to data from Capital One.

It might not be the norm yet, but why not be an early adopter?

Couples are spending less on rings

Getting married is expensive. The average wedding cost $34,200 this year, according to The Knot, and your preference for a more affordable alternative is increasingly commonplace. Wedding rings seem to be an area "where couples have the flexibility," said Emily Forrest Skurnik, a spokesperson for wedding-planning platform Zola.

Lab-grown diamonds are now more popular than natural diamonds for engagement rings, according to Zola's 2026 Wedding Style Report: 54% of couples opt for lab-grown, while only 34% choose natural diamonds.

"This reflects a broader shift toward couples embracing alternatives to traditional wedding jewelry and prioritizing personal preferences over convention," Skurnik said.

I know you're asking about wedding bands but, for context, many couples are spending less on rings altogether. In 2025, Americans spent, on average, $4,600 on an engagement ring, according to data from The Knot. In 2024, they spent $5,200.

Along with a lower price point, DTC brands often offer longer return windows, too. Traditional jewelers usually offer a 14-day to 30-day return window.

At Quince, though, you can return a wedding band for one year and an engagement ring for 60 days. At online jewelry store Frank Darling, shoppers can return or exchange their ring 30 days from when the order is ready to ship or pick up, or 60 days from the date of the first purchase, whichever comes first.

Because Quince's appeal over other DTC brands is that it sells quality products at a discounted price - $50 cashmere, for example - I'd be relatively comfortable purchasing a wedding band from them.

Ask questions

Katherine Bodoh, a registered jeweler and CEO of the American Gem Society, says that before you buy any ring - whether it be from a traditional jeweler or a DTC brand - you should ask a few questions:

-- Is the diamond lab-grown or natural? Does it come with a grading report?

-- What's the return policy, the warranty and the plan for sizing or repairs down the road?

-- Is there a trained gemologist on staff who can help you?

"When you buy from a local jeweler, you can see the piece in person - so online, you want those protections in place," Bodoh said. "And if a price seems too good to be true, the quality may not be what you expect."

Quince offers both lab-grown and natural stones which come with a grading report, the aforementioned return policy and a warranty. It does not offer resizing, and doesn't employ a gemologist. (Representatives for Quince did not respond to requests for comment.)

I know that oftentimes, the logistics of getting engaged and married can take away from the joy of progressing in a partnership. If ordering a ring online makes this experience more stressful, I say use a traditional jeweler. But if you want to spend a bit less, this seems like a great option.

Write to Dollar Signs at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

By submitting your story to Dow Jones & Co., the publisher of MarketWatch, you understand and agree that we may use your story, or versions of it, in all media and platforms.

-Aditi Shrikant

data.title: World Young Scientist Summit 2026 Opens in Wenzhou, Zhejiang
data.description:
World Young Scientist Summit 2026 Opens in Wenzhou, Zhejiang

World Young Scientist Summit 2026 Opens in Wenzhou, Zhejiang

PR Newswire

WENZHOU, China, Oct. 24, 2026

WENZHOU, China, Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- This is a report by China Daily:

On October 24, the World Young Scientist Summit 2026 opened in Wenzhou, Zhejiang. The event is hosted by the China Association for Science and Technology (CAST), the Zhejiang Provincial People's Government, and the World Association of Young Scientists. Nearly 800 representatives, including scientists, educators, and entrepreneurs from more than 60 countries and regions, are attending the summit.

He Junke, Vice President of CAST in charge of daily work and First Secretary of its Secretariat; Lian Yimin, Chairman and Party Group Secretary of the Zhejiang Provincial Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference; Marcelo Knobel, Executive Director of The World Academy of Sciences; and Zhang Zhenfeng, Member of the Standing Committee of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee and Secretary of the CPC Wenzhou Municipal Committee, attended the summit and delivered remarks. Yao Gaoyuan, Vice Governor of the Zhejiang Provincial People's Government, presided over the first segment of the plenary session.

With the theme "Gathering Talents Worldwide to Create a Better Future," the summit's annual agenda is "Global Youth Action in the AI Era: Building a Sustainable Future." It aims to draw on the insights of young people around the world, deepen international sci-tech cooperation, and jointly address questions about young people, science, the world and the future.

Efim Zelmanov, Fields Medalist and Foreign Member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences; Chen Yunji, Deputy Director of the Institute of Computing Technology, CAS, and Director of the National Key Laboratory of Processor Chips; Mary Garson, President of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry; and Lu Chaoyang, Member of the Standing Committee of CAST, Executive Dean of the Shanghai Institute of Advanced Study, University of Science and Technology of China, and Chairman of the Council of the World Association of Young Scientists, delivered keynote speeches respectively on education reform in the AI era, AI and processor chips, young women scientists' participation in science, and quantum computing. They explored new opportunities for scientific research, talent cultivation, and international cooperation in the AI era.

This year's summit placed greater emphasis on the growth needs of young scientists, with young talents under the age of 45 accounting for 88 percent of participants. It aimed to build a cluster of international journals, bring together young scientific talent, facilitate a batch of international collaborative projects and advance the application and commercialization of scientific and technological achievements. The summit released the Report on the Distribution and Mobility of Young Scientists in the Field of Embodied Intelligence, launched the World Young Scientist Summit Partner Journal Program and the 2026 World Young Scientist Innovation and Entrepreneurship Growth Support Program. It also published the "Young Scientist Pioneers 2035" list and announced the 2026 Sustainable Development Young Scientist Award. The awards were presented to four Chinese and foreign scientists.

Chen Tianrun, Founder of Hangzhou Moxin Technology Co., Ltd.; Yuan Yang, Assistant to the Dean of the Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences at Tsinghua University; and two of the 2026 Sustainable Development Young Scientist Award winners, César de la Fuente and Nicola Segata, among other Chinese and foreign young scientist representatives, spoke at the flash-talk session to share their research practices and reflections.

In addition, the conference focused on fields such as future manufacturing, quantum information, embodied intelligence, brain-computer intelligence, environmental science, deep-sea resources, and life and health, and held 12 parallel forums. It also included the "Gravitation π" Future Technology and Concept Products Exhibition and Exchange, local thematic side events, and sci-tech and humanities study visits, further building an interdisciplinary, cross-regional and cross-sector platform for youth sci-tech exchange and cooperation.

data.title: Looking for AI stocks that are still cheap? Consider these two under-the-radar picks.
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

Simon Kim of Saturna Capital names two stocks tied to base metals, for investors who want to look beyond the beaten path for AI-related trades

Komatsu trades much lower relative to sales and earnings estimates than larger rival Caterpillar.

Simon Kim and his co-managers for the Saturna International Fund believe that the artificial-intelligence build-out still has a long way to go, despite market jitters over high valuations. So they are still "overweight AI" but are looking for stocks in related industries that trade at attractive valuations.

The Saturna International Fund SSIFX is rated five stars (the highest rating) within Morningstar's "Foreign Large Growth" category. As of Sept. 30, about 15% of the 40-stock portfolio was invested in U.S. companies, according to Morningstar's data.

During an interview with MarketWatch, Kim named Komatsu (KMTUY) (JP:6301), the Japan-based manufacturer of heavy construction equipment, as an example of a value-priced investment tied to base metals, which he described as an industry that is "tangential to AI."

"Within base metals, there are not a lot of good companies," he said, because mining firms and financiers "have destroyed capital by investing heavily at the wrong times."

'They sit back and collect.'Simon Kim of the Saturna International Fund, on the business strategy of Altius Minerals

"What I am looking for is companies that track the metals price and have compounding alpha on top of that," Kim said.

"You get exposure to the metals price. If the supercycle hits, these companies will benefit," and, if not, you still hold compounding businesses at reasonable valuations, he said.

"Alpha" refers to how much something outperforms its benchmark or market average.

Komatsu and Caterpillar

The Saturna International Fund holds shares of Komatsu that are listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. There is also an American depositary receipt for the company.

Komatsu is Caterpillar's (CAT) main international competitor, although it is a much smaller company, with a market capitalization of $42.6 billion and a consensus 2026 revenue estimate of $28.18 billion for its fiscal year that will end in March, according to a FactSet survey of analysts. In comparison, Caterpillar's market cap is $333.63 billion, and its annual sales for 2026 are estimated to total $79.95 billion.

If we look at the stock price relative to forward sales estimates, based on consensus estimates for the next 12 months among analysts pooled by FactSet, Komatsu's ADR trades at a forward price-to-sales ratio of 1.5, while Caterpillar's stock price is 3.8 times forward sales. And the forward price-to-earnings ratio for Komatsu's ADR is 15, while Caterpillar's forward P/E is 23, according to FactSet.

Now take a look at a one-year chart, which shows better performance for Caterpillar, but a lot less volatility for Komatsu:

Caterpillar's stock has had a higher return than Komatsu's ADR over the past year, but it has been a bumpier ride for "CAT."

For one-year total returns though Monday, with dividends reinvested, Caterpillar takes the prize. But so far in 2026, Komatsu's ADR has returned 47.5%, while Caterpillar has returned 27.5%.

Over the past three years, Caterpillar's stock has returned 202%, while Komatsu's ADR has returned 92%.

According to Kim, Caterpillar "has shot up from power generation, since they sell backup generators (and now primary) for data centers, and demand has been ferocious," while Caterpillar's other business lines have also performed well.

"Komatsu does the same things, except that they are not selling the generators," he said.

Kim estimated that the market was placing a $200 billion valuation on Caterpillar's generator business. According to Caterpillar, power-generation equipment sales were $3.1 billion during the second quarter, providing 15% of total revenue, which came to $20.54 billion.

Kim said Caterpillar's power-generation segment could contribute 20% to 25% of the company's total sales next year, but he is still surprised that the market has been "valuing the rest of the biz at $150 billion."

"So it is either valuing [Caterpillar] incorrectly or Komatsu has some catching up to do."

A royalty play

Kim said that the Saturna International Fund tends to hold stocks for about eight years. He cited Altius Minerals, which is based in St. John's, Newfoundland, as an example of a company that has taken an opportunistic long-term approach to provide financing to mining firms at excellent terms during down periods. The company's main stock listing is on the Toronto Stock Exchange (CA:ALS), but the stock is also traded over-the-counter in the U.S. (ATUSF).

According to Kim, Altius's contrarian strategy under its co-founder and CEO Brian Dalton in the base-metals space has led the strong performance for its stock over long periods. These are total returns through Monday: 

 
Company                               2026  3 years  5 years  10 years  20 years 
Altius Minerals (Toronto listing     36.4%     183%     258%      482%      893% 
Altius Minerals (U.S. OTC            32.3%     173%     216%      445%      693% 
S&P 500                              13.4%      87%      83%      323%      722% 
                                                                 Source: FactSet

You can see that the U.S. over-the-counter shares of Altius haven't performed as well as the main listing on the Toronto exchange. The U.S. OTC shares trade in much lower volumes.

"This is the same business model as a Franco or Wheaton - the royalty model. These companies provide capital to a miner in exchange for future revenues," Kim said, referring to Franco-Nevada (FNV) and Wheaton Precious Metas (WPM).

"They want to use capital when commodity prices are low, and people are looking for cash and they are desperate and giving good terms," he said.

"The interesting thing about this royalty model is it has outperformed base metals, as a sector, over the past couple of decades," he said.

Kim cited down cycles for base metals in 2016 and following Russia's invasion of Ukraine as examples of market disruptions that Altius was able to take advantage of.

"They sit back and collect" while waiting for new opportunities, he said.

Kim said the latest example was in the renewable-energy space. "In 2022 you had all these wind investments, and other power generators starved for capital," while at that time Altius, under Dalton's direction, "was buying up assets left and right."

Subsequent events "proved he was right" because of heavy demand for power for data centers, Kim said.

When asked about the high forward P/E of 54.5 for Altius's stock, which compares with a weighted valuation of 18.9 for the S&P 500 SPX, Kim said that for a mining royalty stock, price-to-book value is a more reasonable way to look at valuations. Altius trades at 2.3 times book value, while the S&P 500 trades at 5.6 times book, according to FactSet.

-Philip van Doorn

data.title: From Private Credit to Fusion Power: New to The Street Show #777 Premieres Tonight on Bloomberg Television
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / October 24, 2026 / Where capital flows, how disease is treated, how entertainment reaches the screen and how the world is powered are all being rewritten at once. Tonight, New to The Street brings four companies working at each of those frontiers to a global business audience as Show #777 premieres at 6:30 p.m. ET on Bloomberg Television as sponsored programming, with distribution across the United States, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and Southeast Asia.

Hosted by Jane King and opening from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Show #777 features executive conversations with Bilal Adam, Chief Executive Officer of Stewards Investment Capital; Cuong Do, President and Chief Executive Officer of BioVie Inc. (NASDAQ:BIVI); William "Bill" Mobley, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of FreeCast, Inc. (NASDAQ:CAST); and Brent Nelson, Executive Chairman of American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN).

"Show #777 is about builders who see what others miss," said Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street. "An investment firm bridging developed and emerging markets. A biotech reporting what it believes is a first in long COVID. A software company turning connections into media businesses. And a fusion company that says it can simply sell power. These are the stories our audience in every region tunes in for. No politics. No current events. Only Opportunities To Consider™."

Inside Show #777

Stewards Investment Capital CEO Bilal Adam Discusses Global Investing, Private Credit and Nasdaq Growth

Bilal Adam, CEO of Stewards Investment Capital, joins Jane King to discuss the firm's international investment strategy, private credit solutions, and commitment to financial inclusion.

With activities spanning South Africa, Mauritius, the United States, and Monaco, Stewards Investment Capital focuses on investment opportunities designed to deliver competitive risk-adjusted returns while supporting economic development.

Adam discusses the firm's investment philosophy and its relationship with Nasdaq-listed Stewards Inc. (Nasdaq:SWRD), a U.S.-based diversified financial platform led by CEO and President Shaun Quin. He also highlights telecommunications infrastructure investments aimed at expanding connectivity and financial inclusion in underserved African communities.

The conversation explores how Stewards Investment Capital provides institutional investors, pension funds, family offices, and high-net-worth individuals with access to private credit, portfolio diversification, and international investment opportunities.

Adam also discusses Mauritius as an international financial hub, the growth of Stewards Inc.'s U.S. business, and the significance of the company's recent Nasdaq Opening Bell ceremony.

Looking ahead, he shares his perspective on investment opportunities across developed and emerging markets and Stewards Investment Capital's long-term vision. Learn more at stewardsinvestment.com.

BioVie Inc. (NASDAQ:BIVI): New Long COVID and Parkinson's Data Take Center Stage

President and CEO Cuong Do reports that BioVie presented results from its ADDRESS-LC trial in long COVID and its SUNRISE-PD trial in Parkinson's disease at the American Neurological Association annual meeting, with the findings published in the peer-reviewed Annals of Neurology. Do says patients treated with investigational oral therapy bezisterim who entered the long COVID trial with a high symptom burden showed clinically relevant and statistically significant improvements in fatigue, malaise and cognitive impairment, or "brain fog."

"This is the first trial that has ever shown to have any impact on long COVID neurological symptoms," Do said, noting that all 12 advisors who reviewed the results urged the company to move quickly to a confirmatory Phase 3 trial. Do says BioVie has been invited to present at the NIH's next RECOVER annual meeting and is seeking a meeting with the FDA on Phase 3 trial design. These findings require confirmation in a Phase 3 trial. Learn more at biovie.com.

FreeCast, Inc. (NASDAQ:CAST): "The Connection Is Just the Beginning"

Founder and CEO William Mobley explains why FreeCast is "not another streaming service." Instead, the company provides the software infrastructure that lets telecom companies, wireless carriers, internet providers, satellite companies and membership organizations launch their own branded entertainment hubs, offering free television, premium subscriptions, sports, advertising and commerce. "They bring the customers," Mobley said. "We bring the media and monetization technology."

Mobley introduces PEAC, FreeCast's metric for "partner-enabled addressable customers," which measures potential distribution reach through enterprise agreements. He is clear that PEAC does not represent active users, paying subscribers or confirmed revenue, and describes the company's job as converting that reach into activated users, transactions and, ultimately, revenue across advertising, subscriptions, pay-per-view, live sports, rentals and commerce. Learn more at freecast.com.

American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN): "Basically, We Sell Power"

Executive Chairman Brent Nelson walks viewers through the Texatron™ Fusion Engine™, an aneutronic fusion platform designed for modular, infrastructure-grade deployment across industrial, commercial, defense and grid-constrained applications. Nelson describes 12 engine models using a deuterium and helium-3 fuel cycle that produces helium-4, with no radioactive waste and no meltdown risk. Using pulsed magnetic confinement created with electricity rather than external magnets, the system harvests excess electrons directly as electrical current for data centers, remote industry, hospitals and medical centers.

"Fusion has been coming for 70 years," Nelson said. "We think that we're the first ones to crack that commercial nut." Learn more at americanfusionenergy.com.

SafeSpace Global: an AI-powered safety and security platform designed to help protect the vulnerable in schools, senior care, addiction treatment, correctional facilities and houses of worship

Acurx Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (NASDAQ:ACXP): developing what could be the first new class of antibiotics in nearly 40 years, with the FDA agreeing to consider a future application for lead drug ibezapolstat based on two planned trials, Pathfinder and Aspire

T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA): completed a strategic refinancing of its Orofino, Idaho data center and added a new appointment to its board of directors

data.title: Young Americans are giving up on car ownership. It's a path to financial freedom for some.
data.description:
By Venessa Wong

With vehicle prices soaring and ownership increasingly out of reach, some young adults are discovering that life without a car leaves them with breathing room to spend on other things

The average car has gotten so expensive that giving one up can provide young Americans with greater control over how they spend their money.

When Nick Renteria moved from Boston to Los Angeles for school, he rented a car for about $350 a month. His parents covered the rental cost while he paid for gas, but he hated sitting in traffic, parking and feeling disconnected from the city.

When he finished his program, Renteria, 24, decided he didn't want a car at all.

He moved to West Hollywood, selecting a neighborhood where he could bike to work, use public transportation and altogether avoid the expense of owning a vehicle.

The decision has paid off over the past two years. While a roommate with a car and a similar income struggled financially, Renteria found he could afford to go out with friends and enjoy the city, even while working part-time jobs.

"L.A. is actually kind of affordable if you don't have a car," he said.

For generations of Americans, owning a car has often been a symbol of independence. But, for some younger adults today, that notion is being turned on its head. The average car has gotten so expensive that giving one up can sometimes translate into gaining something equally important: greater control of how they spend their money.

"L.A. is actually kind of affordable if you don't have a car," said Nick Renteria, who went car-free two years ago.

And there are signs that younger Americans are shifting away from car ownership as a symbol of success.

The share of households younger than 35 that owned a vehicle last year fell to 79.4% from 82.1% in 2019, according to data from the Federal Reserve. Meanwhile, over the same period, vehicle ownership among Americans 75 and older rose to 83% from 80.1%. Younger adults have replaced the oldest Americans as the demographic with the lowest vehicle-ownership rate.

Other data suggest that young people are changing how they get around. Among adults 29 and younger, 48% drove themselves in their own car at least once a month this year, down from 53% in 2023, according to YouGov surveys. Meanwhile the share who rode as passengers increased to 54% from 45%. This was the only method of transportation to become more common among Generation Z adults during this period.

Those surveys gauge transportation habits and not necessarily car ownership. But, taken together with the ownership data, they point to a shift in the relationship between young Americans and personal motor vehicles.

The high cost of car ownership

The financial case for young Americans not owning a car is becoming increasingly compelling.

As the rising cost of vehicles, maintenance, insurance and loan payments deter young Americans from buying cars, many are migrating toward ride-sharing, carpooling and car-sharing options, and using delivery services, instead - and some say they prefer those alternatives to having a car of their own.

New vehicles now sell for more than $50,000, on average, and used cars for $27,000. Meanwhile, those who finance their vehicles face average interest rates of 6.35% for new cars and 11.19% for used cars, pushing up the average monthly payment to $765 for new cars and $542 for used cars, according to Experian.

And purchasing a car is only the beginning. Maintenance and insurance costs have increased dramatically since the pandemic, while gas prices have crossed $4 a gallon, on average, this year due to the war in Iran.

The average annual cost to own and operate a new vehicle is now $12,863, according to AAA.

More on this: Cars have become unaffordable for many Americans. Here's what the numbers show.

For younger Americans navigating a difficult job market, expensive housing and student-loan debt can consume a substantial chunk of income.

In a 2025 survey, common concerns hindering Gen Zers from buying a car included not being able to afford the type of car they wanted (30%), interest rates being too high (32%) and costly maintenance (28%), data shared with MarketWatch by Enterprise Mobility show.

On top of that, remote work and online shopping trends, as well as the proliferation of new delivery services, make it easier to forgo car ownership.

Last month, about one out of five workers ages 25 to 34 worked from home at least some of the time, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Meanwhile, Gen Z adults said online shopping (54%) and working from home (48%) have reduced their need to drive over the past few years, and more than 20% cited rideshare services, according to a Mercury Insurance survey in June.

In a separate poll, 29% of Gen Z members said they have used peer-to-peer car-sharing platforms, and, among them, 43% did so at least biweekly or monthly. Convenience and cost savings were the top reasons given among all survey respondents.

To these young Americans, such options have made owning a car a luxury, not a necessity.

For Xenna Smith, 27, selling her Subaru in Raleigh, N.C., last year was partly a money decision and partly about peace of mind. "I just felt a lot of anxiety," she told MarketWatch.

In addition to safety concerns as driver, "it was just costs and costs and costs," she said.

Now, Smith bikes or rides the bus almost anywhere she needs to go, and walks to buy groceries. Her apartment, which costs $1,500 a month, has a gym, a pool and bike parking.

In a typical month, she now spends less than $40 on transportation for the occasional Lyft and bike maintenance, compared with $600 when she had a car. Through a $25 annual membership at bike advocacy group Oaks and Spokes, she gets her bus pass for free.

While renting a car, ride-hailing apps (like Uber and Lyft), and public transit all come with their own costs, average transportation spending for households with no cars are lower at every income level - including the top 20% of earners - compared with households that own or lease at least one automobile, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

'I can afford my student loans now, my rent's comfortable, and I actually am saving money for once.'Xenna Smith, Raleigh, N.C.

There are tradeoffs. Not having a car makes it harder to see people who live out of town and can require extra effort and be physically demanding, Smith said. She also said she wished drivers would "stop being so aggressive to cyclists."

On the other hand, "I can afford my student loans now, my rent's comfortable and I actually am saving money for once," she said of having gone car-free. "I'm not contributing anything bad to the environment, and I'm making myself better physically."

Smith's experience underscores an important point: Going without a car isn't necessarily about giving something up. For some, it's about deciding what they would rather be able to afford.

When Sabrina Rae Santoro, a 33-year-old entrepreneur, moved from northern Scottsdale, Ariz., to Old Town Scottsdale earlier this year, she decided to give up her Mercedes. The loan payment, insurance, gas and maintenance cost about $1,000 each month, but she was only using the car to drive 20 to 30 miles each week because she normally works from home.

"Anybody that knows me knows, like, I am a car girly," Santoro said, but "I simply ran the numbers and worked out a location where everything that I need is pretty much five to 10 minutes away walking, or a short drive," she told MarketWatch.

Now, Santoro uses the on-site gym at home, has her groceries delivered, and shops on Amazon. To get around, she uses Lyft, which runs $450 to $500 a month. Compared with when she owned her car, "I'm spending half [as much on transportation], and the funny thing is, I still go everywhere I want to go. I don't limit myself," she said. "It's actually an improvement in quality of life. I feel free."

Sabrina Rae Santoro, a 33-year-old entrepreneur, decided to give up her Mercedes and says not owning a car has improved her quality of life. "I feel free," she told MarketWatch.

Living in cities with robust public transportation can ease the transition. "It's been a huge relief" financially and mentally to go car-free and not have to worry about maintenance and repairs, said D.J. Hargrave, a 30-year-old who sold his Honda when he moved to Chicago last year.

Hargrave's car expenses ran about $1,000 per month, and, when he sold his Accord Sport back to the dealership, he had to pay about $3,000 in negative equity.

Now, Hargrave relies on Chicago's network of buses and trains with a $75 monthly pass and spends less than $200 a month on Uber rides.

"Younger generations of consumers are doing a lot of math, and they don't believe that owning things is the way to go, or that they can ever own things to the same extent older generations have, so they make different choices," Jeremy Robb, chief economist at Cox Automotive, told MarketWatch.

As young people also delay getting married and have fewer children, "there are lifestyle choices that may mean they don't need to have a car, especially on the family side," Robb added.

Related: America's renter generation is trying to build wealth by investing in stocks instead of owning a house

Car-industry response

These transportation trends are showing up especially in sales of new cars. Drivers ages 18 to 34 made up 9.7% of new vehicle registrations in August, down from 12.7% five years earlier, according to automotive-data company Mobility Global.

data.title: Young Americans are giving up on car -2-
data.description:
"Younger and less affluent buyers have largely left the new-vehicle market," Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, told MarketWatch. At the moment, the U.S. car industry lacks options below $30,000. The loss of entry-level models such as the Ford Focus, Chevrolet Cruze and Nissan Versa over the past decade has "eliminated several key products that brought first-time buyers into the market," he noted.

Historically, "whenever the U.S. market moved too far upmarket, a new competitor helped rebalance prices," Fiorani said. "In the 1950s, it was Volkswagen. In the 1960s, it was Toyota, followed by Honda in the 1970s. Hyundai arrived in the 1980s, followed by Kia in the 1990s."

However, protectionist regulations and tariffs are currently preventing lower-cost cars from China from entering the U.S. market, eliminating a potential source of entry-level vehicles, he said.

From the archives (April 2026): Americans would love this $25,000 hybrid SUV - but it's not available here yet

It's hard for car companies to "make money on vehicles" that cost less than $30,000 now, Tom Libby, director of loyalty solutions and industry analysis at Mobility Global, told MarketWatch, but recent developments show there is consumer demand.

The Ford Maverick, unveiled in 2021 at $20,000, has "done very, very, very well," he said. It now costs $30,000.

Meanwhile, Slate Auto, the new electric-vehicle startup backed by Jeff Bezos, is taking preorders for trucks with roll-up windows that start at $25,000.

Even at lower prices, car makers will have to confront young consumers who are looking for alternatives to ownership. Dominic Berardi, a 21-year-old student in Orlando, Fla., has a car, but moved downtown and got a job as a server close by "because I was already planning to restructure my life around the transit that exists here, if at all possible."

For Berardi, independence no longer means having a car waiting outside. It means freedom from reliance on one.

data.title: Investors' recent money moves show a preference for lowering risks over boosting rewards
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

Investors have been steadily pouring more money into 'quality' companies than 'momentum' stocks

The AI buildout is not the only thing investors cite as they move toward quality, according to Rene Reyna, Invesco's head of equity ETF strategy.

In a sign that investors are feeling anxious about the outlook for the stock market, they have recently shown a clear preference for "quality" shares, which tend to fare best during periods of broad market declines, over the previously highflying momentum stocks.

The S&P 500 is weighted by companies' market value, which means shares of companies with higher market capitalizations have more influence than those with lower market caps. There are various ways to invest along with the index or to try to outperform it by applying factors to hold subsets of the S&P 500.

If you hold shares of the $818 billion State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust SPY, an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 SPX by holding all of its stocks, you can see how technology stalwarts and rapid growers dominate. The top five holdings of SPY - Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN) and two common-share classes of Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) - make up 30.6% of the portfolio.

There are various exchange-traded funds that include S&P 500 stocks but have different risk profiles, including the lower-risk $99 billion Invesco Equal Weight S&P 500 Index ETF RSP, in which each component is weighted the same, the even-lower-risk $19 billion Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF SPHQ, and the more aggressive $22 billion Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF SPMO.

Rene Reyna, Invesco's head of equity ETF strategy, told MarketWatch that flows of new money into the quality ETF (SPHQ) have been steady for most of this year, with positive flows every month except for August. That month, $680 million flowed out of SPHQ, while $714 million flowed into the momentum ETF (SPMO). But in September, the action was subdued and in the opposite direction, with $3.4 million flowing into SPHQ and $43 million flowing out of SPMO. (See below for what constitutes quality and momentum.)

What might make the quality approach work, for now

During the first half of 2026, the equal-weighted approach fared well, with RSP returning 12%, while the S&P 500 returned 10.2%. But SPHQ did even better with a first-half return of 20.8%, while SPMO shined with a 36% return.

SPHQ holds the 100 stocks among the S&P 500 that rank highest according to a quality score that combines returns on equity, debt-to-book value and an "accruals ratio" of operating assets to total assets. The index tracked by this fund is rebalanced twice a year. Each stock is weighted by the product of its quality score and its market capitalization.

SPMO holds the 100 stocks of companies in the S&P 500 with the highest "momentum scores." Twice a year, the components of the S&P 500 are ranked by how much their prices have risen over the previous 12 months, then scored to take volatility into account. The portfolio is made up of the 20% of companies in the S&P 500 that score highest, which are then weighted by a combination of the momentum score and market capitalization

Here's the latest year-to-date performance chart for the three ETFs and the full S&P 500:

The Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF has underperformed the S&P 500 so far this year. The Invesco Momentum ETF tends to outperform the full index during bull markets, but it can underperform during down periods for the broad market.

The chart shows that SPMO has experienced quite a bit of volatility this year, with prices coming down significantly since June 30.

Longer term, SPMO has been a stellar performer, with a five-year return of 137%, against 83% for the S&P 500 and 75% for SPHQ.

But according to Reyna, SPHQ is the safer play for investors during periods of souring sentiment. When asked how SPHQ might help investors who are questioning whether or not the trillions of dollars being spent on the build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure will eventually be justified through profits, he said that based on meetings with clients, "the challenge appears to be beyond AI."

He said that prior to the latest U.S. consumer-price index report, which showed inflation at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.7%, "we were looking at a low probability for another rate increase" when the Federal Reserve meets next week.

And Reyna said investors were also watching 10-year U.S. Treasury notes BX:TMUBMUSD10Y, which were yielding 5.02% early on Thursday. He said a 6% 10-year yield would represent a "challenge" to investors, who "might want to take a 6% return rather than the risk in the stock market."

When compared with the S&P 500's price movement, SPMO has had 142.48% upside capture over the past year, with 106.4% downside capture, according to Reyna. Meanwhile, SPHQ has had 86.05% upside capture, with only 61.1% downside capture. Basically, you might not make as much with quality relative to momentum when the market is rising, but you also lose a lot less when the market falls.

For investors who wish to stay invested while softening the effect of a possible market correction, the lower-volatility approach has been gaining in popularity.
